text: You've spent this course learning the pieces — Python basics, NumPy, pandas, cleaning, files and databases, and reliable-code habits. The capstone puts them all together on one project, start to finish, the way a working data scientist actually would. Since real company data can't be shared, we'll generate an illustrative retail orders file with NumPy and pandas — deliberately built with the same problems real exports have: mixed date formats, inconsistent text, missing values, absurd outliers, and duplicate rows. A fixed seed means everyone gets identical numbers to work with.

Imagine you've joined an online home-and-lifestyle shop, and the head of sales asks: where does our revenue come from, and are our discounts actually working? That's too vague to code, so sharpen it into two real questions — which regions, categories, and months drive revenue, and do heavily discounted orders contain more items or come back more often as returns. Just as important, define your metric before you look at any data: revenue equals quantity times unit price times one minus the discount, counted only for orders with status complete. Returned and cancelled orders are not revenue.

Set up a project folder that follows the last chapter's habits exactly — a script to generate the data, a data slash raw folder that's never touched by hand, a data slash clean folder for output, a cleaning module, a tests folder, an analysis notebook, and a README. Raw data goes in and stays in data slash raw; cleaned data goes to data slash clean.

Generate the practice file with a seeded NumPy random number generator and 1500 rows — exactly the reproducibility habits from last chapter in action. On top of the clean truth, we deliberately layer in the mess: some dates in U-S format, some in ISO format; some region names uppercased or padded with stray spaces; some prices carrying a dollar sign; some missing quantities and discounts; and a handful of absurd outlier quantities like 999 and negative 2. Thirty rows get duplicated on purpose too.

Load the raw file and interrogate it without changing anything yet. Check its shape — 1,530 rows, 9 columns. Check isna dot sum for missing values column by column. Check duplicated dot sum for exact repeats — 30 of them here. Check the largest quantities, and value underscore counts on region with dropna equals False to see every spelling variant at once.

The audit turns up five real problems. Thirty fully duplicated rows. Missing values scattered across region, quantity, and discount underscore pct. Wrong types — order underscore date and unit underscore price are both stored as text, with prices sometimes carrying a dollar sign and dates arriving in two different formats. Inconsistent text — region shows up as North, NORTH, and space-North-space, all meaning the same thing. And outliers — quantities of 999, 500, and 250, alongside impossible values like 0, negative 1, and negative 2.

Turn every single finding into a written decision before you touch any code. Drop exact duplicate rows outright. Standardize region and status text, labeling a missing region Unknown rather than guessing. Convert prices to real numbers and parse both date formats correctly. Keep only quantities from 1 to 20, a business rule you'd confirm with the shop itself, and drop missing quantities entirely, since revenue simply can't be computed without one. Treat a missing discount as 0, but flag those rows so the fill stays visible. And finally, add revenue and month columns once everything else is clean.

To recap: sharpen a vague request into specific questions and one clearly defined metric. Keep raw data completely untouched, and audit it thoroughly before you clean a single value. Every problem you find becomes a written cleaning decision, not a guess made on the fly. Next lesson, we actually build it.
